accuracy.evidence: Curriculum placement checked against Development Matters (DfE 2021) Communication and Language for 3 and 4 year olds ('use a wider range of vocabulary') and Reception ('learn new vocabulary', 'use new vocabulary through the day'), and the EYFS Speaking ELG. Overextension and underextension are as described by Clark (1973); the 'one name per thing' expectation is Markman's mutual exclusivity bias (1989). Object facts are kept literal and true: a sock goes on before a shoe, cats say miaow, cows moo, sheep baa, horses neigh, a robin is a small bird with a red-orange breast, a daisy has white petals and a yellow centre, a digger digs with an arm and bucket.

misconceptions.evidence: Each scene targets a documented early-vocabulary slip named in the adult text: overextension (the cat, cow, sheep and horse cards are refused from Dog with their own name and sound), underextension (the small dog refused from Not a dog: 'A small dog is still a dog'), refusing a second label (the robin prediction and the challenge 'No, it is a robin' get 'One thing can have two names'), near words (shoe for sock refused with the sock clue) and naming one member for the group (Apple for food refused as 'only one of them').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagexactword is built on naming levels for one object: word-to-picture naming of clothes, a Dog / Not a dog boundary sort for six four-legged animals, choosing the superordinate word for a tray of three pictures, a grown-up-offered exact word dragged onto one of three members of a category (robin among duck and owl), and tapping named things in a drawn park with three birds. It does not sort word cards by a rule or pick opposites (222 flagsortw) or count categories (588 flagcatct); the 6-token shingle gate reports no flag lab above 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds each idea by doing it: the cat bounces out of Dog with 'It has four legs, but it is a cat', the small dog bounces out of Not a dog, the wrong group tag names what the three have in common ('We wear them'), the duck refuses the word robin with the robin's clue, and in the park the exact word is what picks the robin out from the duck and owl. Each DONE line states the rule just used.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: 'Yes, it has four legs' for whether a cat is a dog (the next sort refuses the cat), 'Sock' as the word for sock, hat and coat (the group scene shows the group word is clothes), and 'No, it is a robin, not a bird' (the exact-word scene confirms a robin is a bird too).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions checked in the browser with chal.cjs; each wrong option carries its own slip: over ('Lots of animals have four legs... each has its own name'), only ('One thing can have two names: bird and robin'), one ('Apple is only one of them'), group, near ('A sock is soft and goes on your foot first'), under ('A small dog is still a dog') and vague ('Bird could mean either one. Say the exact word, robin').

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs are short sentences in everyday words for a grown-up to read aloud (Flesch-Kincaid grade below the family kid limit of 5.0); lab cards are one to three words with drawn pictures, and animals carry their sound as a second clue. The adult text stays under the adult limit (8.7) and uses the precise terms: vocabulary, noun, overextension, underextension, mutual exclusivity, group word.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph does one job (naming and near words, the dog boundary, group words, the exact word). Adult paragraphs give curriculum placement, the over/underextension research with what to say, the named mistakes, and what grown-ups and the lab do. The content gate finds no filler phrase.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px phone screenshots in light and dark for all five scenes: the four clothes cards sit 2 by 2 under the word card, the animal card sits above the two boxes whose ticked lists fit, the four group tags fit 2 by 2, Gran's bubble wraps inside its box above three picture cards, and park labels sit on white chips so they stay readable over the tree and grass; the Found tally is dark ink on the light grass in both themes.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: one button per clothes picture naming the word sought, Dog / Not a dog naming the animal's sound, one group-word button naming the three pictures, one button per exact-word picture, and one Tap-the button per park object. The canvas aria-label carries each scene description and every piece of feedback; challenge feedback is a role=status live region; right and wrong carry ✓ and ✗ as well as colour; axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes.

sources: Department for Education (2021) Development Matters: non-statutory curriculum guidance for the EYFS, Communication and Language (3 and 4 year olds; Reception)
